note — the bold part is what the card te: wer asks about a person. The question word comes first, the verb second.
wer: who. Not to be confused with wo, which means where.
wer is the subject here, so the verb takes the er form: kommt.
was asks about a thing.
was first, the verb second, then du: no do-helper.
The stem kost- ends in -t, so er takes -et: kostet.
The verb comes second, right after the question word.
wo asks where something or someone is.
wo + ist: where is.
wo: the place where something is.

English: I have a question: **where** is the station?
German: Ich habe eine Frage: **Wo** ist der Bahnhof?
note — the bold part is what the card te: A full question after a colon starts with a capital letter.
woher is where from in one word, and it stays together at the front.
wohin asks for a direction, where to; wo is only for where something is.
gehen asks wohin, not wo: the movement needs the -hin.
German asks how you are called: wie, not was.
The stem ends in ß, so du adds only -t: du heißt.
er heißt: the same form as du, because the stem already ends in ß.
Wie heißt…? asks for a name: literally how is she called.

English: How do you **like** the flat? (one friend)
note — the bold part is what the card te: The stem ends in -d, so du takes -est. Wie findest du…? asks what someone thinks of something.
wie before an adjective: how old, how big.
wie + adjective, then the verb second.
wann asks about time. Not wenn, which is a different word.
wann first, the verb second, the subject after it.
warum: why. nicht still goes to the end.

English: **Why** are you buying a computer? (one friend)
note — the bold part is what the card te: warum first, then the verb, then du, then the rest.
In a yes/no question the verb comes first, before the subject.
No do-helper: the verb itself opens the question.
The verb first, then Sie: wohnen Sie.
ist first, then the subject die Wohnung.
English needs does; German just moves the verb to the front.
ihr kommt becomes kommt ihr in the question.
The du form keeps its -st when it moves to the front.
The verb first, then Sie.
The verb first: lernst du.
ist first; die Lehrerin is the subject.
To say yes to a negative question, German uses doch; ja would sound like agreeing with the not.

English: Don't you have time? – **Yes**, I do!
German: Hast du keine Zeit? – **Doch**, ich habe Zeit!
note — the bold part is what the card te: doch contradicts the negative: yes, I do have time.

English: Is the cinema expensive? – **No**, it is cheap.
German: Ist das Kino teuer? – **Nein**, es ist billig.
note — the bold part is what the card te: A positive question gets ja or nein; doch is only for negative ones.
